statement: The codebase-design vocabulary and principles are shared guidance consulted whenever code is being designed or restructured, and are explicitly reusable by other skills.

source.quote: description: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.

trigger: a module's interface is being designed, improved, or evaluated for testability, or another procedure needs deep-module vocabulary
outcome: the actor reasons about module depth/seams using a consistent shared vocabulary
notes: The clause 'when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary' is direct evidence this is meant for reuse, not a standalone bounded workflow.
rationale: No single bounded outcome or completion condition is described here (contrast diagnosing-bugs' sequential loop) -- it is vocabulary consumed by other procedures (DEEPENING, DESIGN-IT-TWICE both open with 'Assumes the vocabulary in SKILL.md'), matching the §6.6 shared-context test.

statement: Use the canonical design vocabulary (module, interface, implementation, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality) consistently across all design work rather than looser synonyms.

source.quote: Design **deep modules**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. Use this language and these principles wherever code is being designed or restructured. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

trigger: code is being designed or restructured
outcome: design discussion and artifacts use one consistent vocabulary
rationale: A terminology-consistency rule reused across every design-adjacent procedure; not itself a checkpoint or a bounded procedure.

statement: When naming design concepts, use the glossary's exact terms and avoid generic substitutes such as 'component,' 'service,' 'API,' or 'boundary.'

source.quote: Use these terms exactly — don't substitute "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Consistent language is the whole point.

trigger: a design concept is named in conversation or written artifacts
outcome: terminology stays consistent across callers, tests, and reviewers
rationale: Same class as BU-P4-002: a naming-discipline rule, not a checkpoint.

statement: Depth is judged at a module's interface, not its implementation: a module can be internally composed of small, swappable parts as long as those parts stay out of the external interface.

source.quote: - **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts — they just aren't part of the interface. A module can have **internal seams** (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the **external seam** at its interface.

trigger: assessing whether a module is well-shaped
outcome: the assessment focuses on interface surface, not internal structure
rationale: A design heuristic applied during judgment, not a mechanical/deterministic check -- reused wherever depth is assessed.

statement: To judge whether a piece of code is pulling its weight as a separate module, imagine deleting it: if its complexity vanishes it was a pass-through, if the complexity reappears across every caller it was earning its keep.

source.quote: - **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep.

trigger: deciding whether a module or seam is justified
outcome: a concrete pass/fail heuristic for module justification
rationale: Named, reusable heuristic ('the deletion test') consulted during design judgment across multiple procedures.

statement: A module's interface is also its test surface: if a test needs to reach past the interface to verify behavior, the module's shape is probably wrong.

source.quote: - **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.

trigger: writing or reviewing tests against a module
outcome: test placement is used as a diagnostic for interface quality
rationale: Reused testing heuristic, echoed again in DEEPENING.md's testing-strategy section (BU-P4-016).

statement: Do not introduce a seam (an interface point where behavior can be swapped) unless at least two things actually vary across it; a seam with only one implementation is unjustified indirection.

source.quote: - **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

trigger: considering whether to add an interface/seam at a boundary
outcome: seams are added only when justified by real variation
notes: Restated near-verbatim in DEEPENING.md's 'Seam discipline' section (BU-P4-014); both should map to the same shared-context entry.
rationale: A durable design rule reused by the DEEPENING sub-procedure almost word for word -- strong shared-context-map evidence.

statement: When designing for testability, have the module accept its dependencies as parameters rather than constructing them internally.

source.quote: 1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

trigger: shaping a module's interface for testability
outcome: dependencies are injectable, enabling substitution in tests
rationale: One of three concrete testability sub-rules; small enough to stand as its own unit.

statement: When designing for testability, have functions return results rather than mutate shared state as a side effect.

source.quote: 2. **Return results, don't produce side effects.**

trigger: shaping a module's interface for testability
outcome: behavior is verifiable by inspecting a returned value, not by inspecting mutated state
rationale: Second of three testability sub-rules.

statement: Keep a module's interface small: fewer methods and simpler parameters both reduce the number and complexity of tests needed.

source.quote: 3. **Small surface area.** Fewer methods = fewer tests needed. Fewer params = simpler test setup.

trigger: shaping a module's interface for testability
outcome: interface size is treated as a direct driver of test cost
rationale: Third of three testability sub-rules.

statement: Reject 'depth as the ratio of implementation lines to interface lines' as the definition of module depth, because it rewards padding the implementation; use depth-as-leverage (behavior obtainable per unit of interface learned) instead.

source.quote: - **Depth as ratio of implementation-lines to interface-lines** (Ousterhout): rewards padding the implementation. We use depth-as-leverage instead.

trigger: defining what 'depth' means for this vocabulary
outcome: a specific competing metric is explicitly excluded, with the reason recorded
notes: Functions like a miniature embedded ADR (a rejected alternative recorded with its rationale) inside the glossary itself; compare to the domain-modeling ADR convention (BU-P4-041, BU-P4-046).
rationale: A recorded rejected-alternative decision about the vocabulary itself, not a checkpoint or workflow.

statement: Do not use 'boundary' as a synonym for 'seam' or 'interface,' because 'boundary' is already overloaded by Domain-Driven Design's 'bounded context.'

source.quote: - **"Boundary"**: overloaded with DDD's bounded context. Say **seam** or **interface**.

trigger: choosing vocabulary for design discussion
outcome: a specific term is excluded from the vocabulary, with the conflicting meaning it would create named explicitly
rationale: Same class as BU-P4-011: a rejected-term decision recorded with rationale.

statement: Deepening a cluster of shallow modules is a distinct, bounded procedure: classify the cluster's dependencies, apply seam discipline, and replace old tests with tests at the new deepened interface.

source.quote:
# Deepening

How to deepen a cluster of shallow modules safely, given its dependencies. Assumes the vocabulary in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) — **module**, **interface**, **seam**, **adapter**.

trigger: a cluster of modules is identified as shallow and a candidate for deepening
outcome: the cluster is merged/restructured into a deeper module with tests at its new interface
notes: 'deepen-module' is a builder-assigned candidate workflow name synthesizing DEEPENING.md + DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md's shared procedure; it is not a literal upstream artifact name.
rationale: Has a recognizable trigger (a shallow cluster is identified), a bounded outcome (a deepened module with a chosen dependency-testing strategy), and a completion condition (old tests replaced) -- the §6.2 test for a reusable procedural outcome.
alternatives_considered: stage-context under codebase-design (rejected: codebase-design names a skill family, not a single owning workflow or stage this could attach to as guidance — deepening has its own trigger and multi-step bounded outcome)
shared-context (rejected: classify-dependencies/apply-seam-discipline/replace-tests is a one-time procedural sequence belonging to this workflow, not a rule consulted by other workflows)

statement: When a deepening candidate's dependencies are pure in-process computation with no I/O, always merge the modules and test the result directly through the new interface; no adapter is needed.

source.quote: Pure computation, in-memory state, no I/O. Always deepenable — merge the modules and test through the new interface directly. No adapter needed.

trigger: a deepening candidate's dependencies are classified as in-process
outcome: the modules are merged and tested at the new interface with no adapter layer
rationale: A judgment checkpoint (classify then act) inside the deepen-module procedure.

statement: When a deepening candidate depends on something with a local test stand-in (e.g. an in-memory filesystem or an in-process database emulator), deepening is possible and the deepened module is tested against that stand-in inside the test suite, with the seam kept internal.

source.quote: Dependencies that have local test stand-ins (PGLite for Postgres, in-memory filesystem). Deepenable if the stand-in exists. The deepened module is tested with the stand-in running in the test suite. The seam is internal; no port at the module's external interface.

trigger: a deepening candidate's dependencies are classified as local-substitutable
outcome: the deepened module is tested with the stand-in, without exposing a port at the external interface
rationale: Selects the correct adapter-free testing strategy for one dependency category during the classify-dependencies stage; matching a dependency against a local stand-in is judgment applied while classifying, not a deterministic script action, so it stays stage-context rather than dropping to helper.

statement: When a deepening candidate depends on the team's own remote services, define a port (interface) at the seam owned by the deep module, inject an in-memory adapter for tests and an HTTP/gRPC/queue adapter for production.

source.locator: Dependency categories / Remote but owned, L19
source.quote: Your own services across a network boundary (microservices, internal APIs). Define a **port** (interface) at the seam. The deep module owns the logic; the transport is injected as an **adapter**. Tests use an in-memory adapter. Production uses an HTTP/gRPC/queue adapter.

trigger: a deepening candidate's dependencies are classified as remote-but-owned
outcome: logic lives in one deep module; transport is swappable via an injected adapter
rationale: Requires judging whether a dependency counts as 'remote but owned' and choosing the port/adapter shape accordingly; that is actor judgment exercised during classify-dependencies, not a mechanical file operation, so helper is rejected in favor of stage-context.

statement: When a deepening candidate depends on a true third-party external service the team doesn't control, inject that dependency as a port and give tests a mock adapter.

source.quote: Third-party services (Stripe, Twilio, etc.) you don't control. The deepened module takes the external dependency as an injected port; tests provide a mock adapter.

trigger: a deepening candidate's dependencies are classified as true-external
outcome: the module is testable without calling the real third-party service
rationale: Same class as BU-P4-016: recognizing a 'true external' dependency and choosing a mock-adapter strategy is a judgment call made while classifying dependencies, not a deterministic helper action.

statement: Do not introduce a port at a deepened module's seam unless at least two adapters (typically production and test) are actually justified; a single-adapter seam is unjustified indirection.

source.quote: - **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a port unless at least two adapters are justified (typically production + test). A single-adapter seam is just indirection.

trigger: deciding whether to expose a port at a deepened module's seam
outcome: ports are added only when at least two real adapters justify them
notes: Near-verbatim restatement of BU-P4-007 from SKILL.md, in the ports-and-adapters vocabulary.
rationale: Same underlying rule as BU-P4-007, duplicated across two source files -- direct evidence for the shared-context-map, not a second independent behavior.

statement: A deep module may have internal seams used only by its own tests as well as its external interface seam; internal seams should not be exposed through the public interface merely because tests happen to use them.

source.quote: - **Internal seams vs external seams.** A deep module can have internal seams (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the external seam at its interface. Don't expose internal seams through the interface just because tests use them.

trigger: deciding what to expose on a deepened module's public interface
outcome: internal test seams stay internal; the public interface is not widened to accommodate them
rationale: A design-discipline rule about what belongs on a public interface, reused wherever a deepened module's seams are being decided -- not a mechanical check with one right answer, so it stays shared-context rather than helper.

statement: After deepening a module, delete the old unit tests that targeted the now-merged shallow modules rather than keeping them alongside new interface-level tests.

source.quote: - Old unit tests on shallow modules become waste once tests at the deepened module's interface exist — delete them.

trigger: a deepened module's new interface-level tests exist
outcome: the shallow modules' old unit tests are removed rather than retained
rationale: A specific action within the test-at-new-interface stage that depends on the actor's judgment about which old tests now target the merged modules; identifying that scope is not a fully deterministic file-deletion helper.

statement: Tests written against a deepened module must assert on observable outcomes through the interface, not on internal state, so they survive internal refactors; a test that must change when the implementation changes is testing past the interface.

source.quote: - Tests should survive internal refactors — they describe behaviour, not implementation. If a test has to change when the implementation changes, it's testing past the interface.

trigger: writing tests for a deepened module
outcome: tests remain green across internal refactors that don't change observable behavior
notes: Same class of heuristic as BU-P4-006 ('the interface is the test surface').
rationale: A testing-discipline check applied while writing the new interface-level tests in this stage; judging whether a test reaches past the interface requires actor discretion, not a mechanical rule, so it remains stage-context rather than helper.

statement: When exploring alternative interfaces for a chosen deepening candidate, run a parallel-sub-agent pattern that produces several radically different designs before picking one, on the premise that a single first idea is unlikely to be the best.

source.quote: When the user wants to explore alternative interfaces for a chosen deepening candidate, use this parallel sub-agent pattern. Based on "Design It Twice" (Ousterhout) — your first idea is unlikely to be the best.

trigger: a deepening candidate has been chosen and alternative interface shapes should be explored before committing
outcome: multiple independently-produced interface designs exist and are compared before one is chosen
rationale: A real durable checkpoint per the §6.3 test: whether this is implemented by spawning literal sub-agents, running sequential design passes, or any other mechanism, the outcome operators would care about -- 'were multiple genuinely different designs compared before committing' -- still exists.
alternatives_considered: stage-context (rejected: whether multiple independently-produced designs were compared before committing is a durable, checkable outcome in its own right, not guidance folded into another stage)

helper (rejected: producing and comparing genuinely different interface designs is judgment work — recognizing when an idea is radically different, not just cosmetically so — not a deterministic subordinate mechanic)

statement: Before spawning parallel design sub-agents, first produce and show the user a framing of the problem space (constraints, dependency category, an illustrative sketch), then proceed immediately to spawning sub-agents without waiting for a reply.

source.quote: Show this to the user, then immediately proceed to Step 2. The user reads and thinks while the sub-agents work in parallel.

trigger: framing has been produced for a design-it-twice pass
outcome: the user is informed of the problem framing concurrently with sub-agent work starting, rather than gating on their reply
notes: Notably NOT a needs_input-style blocking checkpoint -- the actor shows context and proceeds without waiting.
rationale: Sequencing guidance for the design-it-twice stage (frame first, then spawn without waiting) that only makes sense embedded in that stage's own flow; it is not a reusable mechanical step outside this stage, so stage-context is preferred over helper.

statement: Produce at least three independently-generated, radically different interface designs for the same deepening candidate, each under an explicit distinguishing design constraint (e.g. minimal interface, maximal flexibility, optimize the common case, ports-and-adapters).

source.quote: Spawn 3+ sub-agents in parallel using the Agent tool. Each must produce a **radically different** interface for the deepened module.

trigger: the problem space has been framed for a design-it-twice pass
outcome: three or more genuinely distinct candidate interface designs exist for comparison
notes: 'using the Agent tool' is the mechanism (Old Sergeant's/Claude Code's own native sub-agent spawning capability); the durable intent is 'produce several independently-generated, distinct designs,' not the specific spawning API. This is fully expressible today as an ordinary actor-stage instruction -- the native harness already owns its own sub-agent tool, so Sergeant's engine needs nothing new here.
rationale: Mechanism (a specific tool call) vs. intent (independently-generated diverse designs) -- the intent is durable, the Agent-tool mechanism is incidental to whichever harness is selected.

statement: Each parallel design sub-agent's brief must include both the module-design vocabulary (module/interface/seam/adapter) and the project's domain glossary vocabulary, so every generated design uses consistent architecture and domain language.

source.quote: Include both [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) vocabulary and CONTEXT.md vocabulary in the brief so each sub-agent names things consistently with the architecture language and the project's domain language.

trigger: briefing a parallel design sub-agent
outcome: generated designs are internally consistent with both the architecture vocabulary and the project's domain vocabulary
notes: Direct evidence of shared-context reuse across two different skill/context sources (codebase-design's SKILL.md and domain-modeling's CONTEXT.md) inside one stage's brief.
rationale: Explicit cross-reference to another shared-context source (CONTEXT.md); strong shared-context-map evidence.

statement: Present the several generated interface designs to the user one at a time so each can be absorbed, then compare them explicitly by depth (leverage at the interface), locality (where change concentrates), and seam placement, ending with an opinionated recommendation (including a hybrid if warranted) rather than a menu.

source.quote:
Present designs sequentially so the user can absorb each one, then compare them in prose. Contrast by **depth** (leverage at the interface), **locality** (where change concentrates), and **seam placement**.

After comparing, give your own recommendation: which design you think is strongest and why. If elements from different designs would combine well, propose a hybrid. Be opinionated — the user wants a strong read, not a menu.

trigger: multiple candidate designs have been produced
outcome: the user receives a structured comparison and a concrete recommendation, not a raw dump of options
rationale: Directs how the design-it-twice stage presents and judges the sub-agent outputs -- a comparative judgment call (depth/locality/seam, then an opinionated pick) specific to that stage, not a deterministic helper action.

statement: Domain-modeling guidance (glossary discipline, ADR criteria) is reusable actor context invoked whenever any procedure needs to build or maintain the project's domain model, not only when the user directly asks for it.

source.quote: description: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.

trigger: any procedure needs to pin down terminology or record an architectural decision
outcome: the domain glossary and ADR log stay current as a side effect of ordinary design/spec/ticket work
notes: 'or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model' is direct textual reuse evidence, echoed by to-spec (BU-P4-050) and DESIGN-IT-TWICE (BU-P4-025) both consuming CONTEXT.md.
rationale: No bounded completion condition of its own; it is consumed by other workflows exactly like codebase-design's vocabulary (BU-P4-001).

statement: Domain modeling is an active, continuous discipline exercised while other work happens: challenge terminology, invent edge-case scenarios, and write glossary/decision updates down the moment they crystallize, rather than only reading the existing glossary passively.

source.quote: Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline — challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill — that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

trigger: the domain model is being actively built or sharpened during a design conversation
outcome: glossary/ADR updates happen inline, not batched
rationale: Describes an ongoing mode of conduct, not a bounded procedure with a completion condition.

statement: A repository's domain glossary is either a single root CONTEXT.md (single context) or, when a root CONTEXT-MAP.md exists, split into per-context CONTEXT.md files that the map points to.

source.quote:
Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

trigger: resolving where a project's domain glossary lives
outcome: the correct CONTEXT.md file for the current topic is located
rationale: A deterministic file-resolution rule, not a judgment call.

statement: Create CONTEXT.md and docs/adr/ lazily: only when there is a first term or first decision to record, not upfront.

source.quote: Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

trigger: a term or architectural decision needs recording but the target file doesn't exist yet
outcome: the file is created at first-need rather than scaffolded speculatively
notes: Same lazy-creation policy is restated in ADR-FORMAT.md (BU-P4-041) for docs/adr/ specifically.
rationale: A mechanical file-creation-timing rule (create only at first need) reused across both CONTEXT.md and docs/adr/ -- purely deterministic, so shared-helper over shared-context; and it applies across the whole domain-modeling discipline rather than one workflow, so shared- rather than a plain helper.

statement: When the user's terminology conflicts with the existing glossary, surface the conflict immediately rather than silently accepting the new usage or silently keeping the old definition.

source.quote: When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

trigger: the user uses a term that conflicts with an existing CONTEXT.md definition
outcome: the conflict is named and resolved with the user rather than left ambiguous
rationale: Actor-judgment rule reused wherever domain terms surface, across many parent workflows.

statement: When the user uses a vague or overloaded term, propose a precise canonical replacement rather than proceeding with the ambiguity.

source.quote: When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

trigger: vague or overloaded terminology is used in conversation
outcome: a precise canonical term is proposed and, if accepted, becomes the glossary entry
rationale: Recognizing 'vague or overloaded' language and proposing a precise replacement is a judgment call exercised throughout any conversation touching the domain model, not a deterministic step, so shared-context rather than helper.

statement: When domain relationships are discussed, actively invent edge-case scenarios that force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts, rather than accepting a first informal description.

source.quote: When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

trigger: domain relationships between concepts are being discussed
outcome: boundary cases are resolved explicitly rather than left implicit
rationale: Inventing edge-case scenarios to sharpen a domain relationship is open-ended judgment, reused across whichever workflow is doing domain modeling at the time -- not reducible to a mechanical helper action.

statement: When the user describes how something works, cross-check that description against the actual code, and surface any contradiction found rather than recording the user's account uncritically.

source.quote: When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"

trigger: the user states a domain behavior claim
outcome: any code/description contradiction is surfaced for resolution rather than silently recorded
rationale: Cross-checking a user's description against the actual code and deciding whether a contradiction exists is a judgment call, not a deterministic comparison, so shared-context rather than helper.

statement: When a term is resolved, update CONTEXT.md at that moment rather than batching glossary updates for later.

source.quote: When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up — capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

trigger: a glossary term's definition is resolved during a conversation
outcome: CONTEXT.md reflects the resolved definition immediately
rationale: A timing discipline ('update now, don't batch') governing when the actor acts rather than what file operation to perform -- a habit of conduct reused across the domain-modeling discipline, closer to shared-context than to a scripted helper action.

statement: CONTEXT.md must contain domain glossary content only -- no implementation details, no spec content, no scratch notes -- so it cannot be treated as a spec or a repository for implementation decisions.

source.quote: `CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

trigger: content is about to be added to CONTEXT.md
outcome: CONTEXT.md stays a pure glossary, distinct from spec or implementation-decision content
notes: A hard content-boundary rule -- close to mechanical, hence shared-helper rather than shared-context.
rationale: A hard content-boundary rule (glossary content only, no implementation/spec/scratch) that is close to a mechanical check ('is this content in scope for CONTEXT.md?') rather than an open-ended judgment call, which is why it lands as shared-helper over shared-context; it is reused across every workflow that touches CONTEXT.md, which rules out a workflow-local helper.

statement: Offer to create an ADR only when all three hold: the decision is hard to reverse, it would be surprising to a future reader without context, and it resulted from a genuine trade-off among real alternatives; skip the offer if any one is missing.

source.quote:
Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

trigger: a decision has just been made during design work
outcome: an ADR is offered only for decisions meeting all three criteria, avoiding ADR noise
notes: Restated verbatim (as its own primary source) in ADR-FORMAT.md; see BU-P4-046 for the duplicate.
rationale: A three-part gating test for a durable artifact (the ADR); reused across two source files.

statement: ADRs are numbered sequentially in docs/adr/ (0001-slug.md, 0002-slug.md, ...), with the directory created lazily only when the first ADR is needed.

source.quote:
ADRs live in `docs/adr/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc.

Create the `docs/adr/` directory lazily — only when the first ADR is needed.

trigger: an ADR is being written
outcome: ADRs live in a consistent, sequentially-numbered location
notes: Same lazy-creation policy as BU-P4-030.
rationale: A deterministic filesystem convention (numbering scheme plus lazy directory creation) with no judgment involved, reused by every ADR-writing procedure -- shared-helper, not a workflow-local helper.

statement: An ADR's minimum viable form is a single short paragraph stating the context, the decision, and the reason -- the value is in recording that and why a decision was made, not in filling out template sections.

source.quote: That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why* — not in filling out sections.

trigger: an ADR is being drafted
outcome: a minimal one-paragraph ADR is an acceptable, complete artifact
rationale: States a fixed minimum acceptable form for an ADR -- a deterministic completeness bar, not a judgment call -- reused across every ADR regardless of which workflow produced it, so shared- rather than workflow-local helper.

statement: Optional ADR sections (Status frontmatter, Considered Options, Consequences) are included only when they add genuine value; most ADRs should omit them.

source.quote:
## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`) — useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options** — only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences** — only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

trigger: an ADR is being drafted and might need extra sections
outcome: ADRs stay minimal by default; extra sections are opt-in, not default
rationale: A deterministic default (omit optional sections unless they add genuine value) governing ADR content shared by every ADR-writing procedure, not scoped to one workflow's helper.

statement: To number a new ADR, scan docs/adr/ for the highest existing sequence number and increment by one.

source.quote: Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

trigger: a new ADR file is being created
outcome: the new ADR gets the next sequential number with no gaps or collisions
rationale: A purely mechanical numbering procedure (scan and increment) with one correct answer, reused wherever an ADR is created -- shared-helper, not a judgment-bearing shared-context or a single-workflow helper.

statement: If a decision is easy to reverse, unsurprising, or had no genuine alternative, do not write an ADR for it -- there is nothing beyond 'we did the obvious thing' to record.

source.locator: When to offer an ADR, L37
source.quote: If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it — you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

trigger: deciding whether a just-made decision merits an ADR
outcome: low-value ADRs are avoided by construction
notes: Rationale supporting the same 3-part test as BU-P4-037; duplicate-of BU-P4-037.
rationale: Deciding whether a decision is 'easy to reverse, unsurprising, or lacked a genuine alternative' requires judgment about the decision's nature, not a mechanical check, so shared-context rather than helper; it restates BU-P4-037's three-part test as a negative filter, reused wherever ADRs are considered.

statement: Record rejected alternatives when the rejection reasoning is non-obvious (e.g. choosing REST over GraphQL for subtle reasons), so the same alternative is not re-proposed later without knowledge of why it was already rejected.

source.quote: - **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it — otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

trigger: a non-obvious alternative was considered and rejected during a decision
outcome: the rejection reasoning is preserved so it isn't re-litigated from scratch later
rationale: Judging whether a rejection's reasoning is 'non-obvious' enough to warrant recording is a discretionary call about future readers' likely confusion, not a deterministic rule, so shared-context over helper.

statement: When multiple words exist for the same domain concept, pick one canonical term for the glossary and list the rejected synonyms under an explicit 'Avoid' note on that entry.

source.quote: - **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.

trigger: a glossary entry is being written and synonyms exist
outcome: the glossary picks one term per concept and records the rejected synonyms alongside it
rationale: A mechanical glossary-formatting convention (pick one canonical term, list rejects under an Avoid note) with a fixed structure, reused across every CONTEXT.md entry regardless of workflow -- shared-helper, not a workflow-local helper.

statement: Keep glossary definitions to one or two sentences describing what the term IS, not what it does.

source.quote: - **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.

trigger: a glossary entry is being written
outcome: definitions stay short and identity-focused rather than behavioral
rationale: A fixed formatting constraint (one or two sentences, define what a term IS not what it does) applied mechanically to every glossary entry across the discipline, not scoped to one workflow's helper.

statement: Only add a glossary term if it is specific to this project's domain context; exclude general programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) even if heavily used, by asking whether the concept is unique to this context or a general programming concept.

source.quote: - **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. Before adding a term, ask: is this a concept unique to this context, or a general programming concept? Only the former belongs.

trigger: deciding whether a candidate term belongs in the glossary
outcome: the glossary stays scoped to domain-specific vocabulary, not general engineering vocabulary
rationale: A scoping filter that requires a judgment question each time, not a purely mechanical check.

statement: Group glossary terms under subheadings when natural clusters emerge; a flat list is acceptable if all terms belong to one cohesive area.

source.quote: - **Group terms under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge. If all terms belong to a single cohesive area, a flat list is fine.

trigger: a glossary is being organized
outcome: glossary layout reflects natural conceptual clusters without forcing structure where none exists
rationale: A mechanical layout rule (group under subheadings only when clusters are natural) applied the same way to every CONTEXT.md regardless of which workflow is editing it -- shared-helper, not workflow-local.

statement: Whether a repository has one domain context (single root CONTEXT.md) or several (a root CONTEXT-MAP.md pointing at per-context CONTEXT.md files) is inferred by which of those files exist; if neither exists, create a root CONTEXT.md lazily at the first resolved term.

source.quote:
The skill infers which structure applies:

- If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, read it to find contexts
- If only a root `CONTEXT.md` exists, single context
- If neither exists, create a root `CONTEXT.md` lazily when the first term is resolved

trigger: resolving which CONTEXT.md file governs the current topic
outcome: the correct single- or multi-context structure is used without manual reconfiguration
rationale: A deterministic file-existence check (which of CONTEXT.md/CONTEXT-MAP.md exists) that resolves the glossary's structure without judgment, reused by every procedure that needs to locate it -- shared-helper, not a single workflow's helper.

statement: When multiple domain contexts exist and it's unclear which one the current topic belongs to, ask the user rather than guessing.

source.quote: When multiple contexts exist, infer which one the current topic relates to. If unclear, ask.

trigger: multiple CONTEXT.md contexts exist and the current topic's owning context is ambiguous
outcome: context ambiguity is resolved by asking rather than by silent assumption
rationale: A fail-closed-style rule (ambiguity routes to a question, not a guess) at the authoring-convention level.

statement: Turning the current conversation into a published spec is a synthesis-only procedure: do not interview the user, and instead write the spec from what has already been discussed and from codebase exploration.

source.quote:
description: Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the project issue tracker — no interview, just synthesis of what you've already discussed.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

This skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a spec (you may know this document as a PRD). Do NOT interview the user — just synthesize what you already know.

trigger: the user asks to turn the current conversation into a spec/PRD
outcome: a spec is published to the issue tracker without a separate interview pass
notes: Explicitly distinguishes this workflow from an interview-driven one (contrast wayfinder's grilling ticket type, BU-P4-081).
rationale: Recognizable trigger (turn conversation into spec), bounded outcome (published spec issue with a triage label), and completion condition (publication) -- the §6.2 test.
alternatives_considered: stage (rejected: to-spec has its own trigger phrase and is invoked directly by the user, independent of any other procedure — it is not entered as a step of a larger workflow)
shared-context (rejected: the no-interview/synthesis-only constraint defines this workflow's own procedure, it is not a rule multiple workflows consult)

statement: Before drafting a spec, explore the repository to understand current state (if not already done), and use the project's domain glossary vocabulary and respect any ADRs in the touched area throughout the spec.

source.quote: 1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven't already. Use the project's domain glossary vocabulary throughout the spec, and respect any ADRs in the area you're touching.

trigger: a spec is about to be drafted
outcome: the spec is grounded in current codebase state and consistent with the project's glossary/ADRs
notes: Direct reuse of domain-modeling's CONTEXT.md/ADR outputs (BU-P4-027, BU-P4-037).
rationale: Directs how the gather-context stage of to-spec should ground itself (explore if needed, reuse glossary/ADR vocabulary) -- guidance the actor applies while performing that stage's own judgment, not a deterministic action, so stage-context rather than helper.

statement: Before writing a spec's implementation section, sketch out the seams at which the feature will be tested, preferring existing seams and the highest possible seam, aiming for as few new seams as possible (ideally exactly one).

source.quote: 2. Sketch out the seams at which you're going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.

trigger: a spec's testing/implementation shape is being decided
outcome: the spec commits to a minimal, high-leverage seam plan before publication
notes: Reuses codebase-design's 'seam' vocabulary and the one-adapter/two-adapter discipline (BU-P4-007, BU-P4-018).
rationale: The seam-minimization heuristic applied specifically while sketching a spec's test seams in this stage -- a design judgment call (which seam is highest/existing), not a scripted step, so stage-context over helper.

statement: After sketching test seams for a spec, confirm with the user that the proposed seams match their expectations before finalizing the spec.

source.quote: Check with the user that these seams match their expectations.

trigger: candidate test seams have been sketched for a spec
outcome: the seam plan is user-confirmed before the spec is written and published
notes: A judgment checkpoint requiring the user; representable today via the existing needs_input-class Work state, not an engine gap.
rationale: A user-confirmation checkpoint embedded in the sketch-seams stage's own flow, representable today as an ordinary needs_input round-trip within that stage rather than a separate durable stage or an engine capability (adjudication A13 confirms this reading over X8's engine-gap framing) -- stage-context, not helper, because it requires the user's judgment, not a mechanical step.

statement: Write the spec using the fixed spec template, publish it to the project issue tracker, and apply the ready-for-agent triage label without requiring additional triage.

source.quote: 3. Write the spec using the template below, then publish it to the project issue tracker. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label - no need for additional triage.

trigger: the spec content is finalized
outcome: a published, triage-labeled spec issue exists
notes: Cross-references the triage skill's label vocabulary (P3 partition, AGENT-BRIEF.md/triage/SKILL.md).
rationale: Names the write-and-publish stage's overall action (write from template, publish, apply one fixed label) at the stage-instruction level rather than as one deterministic helper step, because it composes several of that stage's own helper-level actions (BU-P4-055/056/057) into the stage's guidance.

statement: The spec template's Implementation Decisions section must not include specific file paths or code snippets, because they go stale quickly.

source.quote: Do NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.

trigger: the Implementation Decisions section of a spec is being written
outcome: the spec stays durable as the codebase changes around it
rationale: A fixed formatting constraint on one section of the to-spec template -- deterministic, no judgment -- but specific to to-spec's own spec-template rather than reused by other workflows' documents, so helper rather than shared-helper.

statement: As a narrow exception to the no-code-snippets rule, if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (a state machine, reducer, schema, or type shape), inline the trimmed decision-relevant part of that snippet and note that it came from a prototype.

source.quote: Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts — not a working demo, just the important bits.

trigger: a prior prototype exists and encodes a decision precisely
outcome: a trimmed, attributed snippet is inlined instead of prose alone
notes: Cross-references the prototype skill (P3 partition) as an upstream source of evidence.
rationale: A narrow, deterministic exception to BU-P4-055's rule, scoped entirely to to-spec's own template -- not a convention any other workflow's helper reuses, so helper rather than shared-helper.

statement: The spec template requires an extensive, numbered list of user stories in the form 'As a <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>' covering all aspects of the feature.

source.quote:
A LONG, numbered list of user stories. Each user story should be in the format of:

1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>

<user-story-example>
1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending
</user-story-example>

This list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.

trigger: the User Stories section of a spec is being written
outcome: the spec captures feature scope as an extensive set of concrete user stories
rationale: A fixed structural requirement of to-spec's own template (numbered user-story format, exhaustive coverage) -- mechanical and specific to this one workflow's document, not reused elsewhere, so helper rather than shared-helper.

statement: Turning a plan, spec, investigation, findings register, PR, or conversation into implementation-ready tracked tickets is a distinct, triggerable procedure with its own dependency-aware breakdown and publication steps.

source.quote:
description: Use when the user says "to tickets", "create issues", "create td tasks", "make epics", or asks to break a plan, spec, investigation, findings register, PR, or conversation into dependency-aware tracer-bullet work for Sergeant and td.
---

trigger: the user asks to convert planning material into tracked tickets
outcome: a dependency-aware set of tickets/epics is published and reported
rationale: Clear trigger phrases, a bounded outcome (published epics/tickets with a reported dispatch frontier), and a completion condition (graph validated) -- the §6.2 test.
alternatives_considered: stage (rejected: to-tickets has its own trigger phrases ('to tickets', 'create issues', etc.) and is independently invocable, not a step folded into another workflow)
shared-context (rejected: the dependency-aware breakdown and publication steps are this workflow's own procedure, not a rule reused by other workflows)

statement: Prefer vertical slices that each produce independently verifiable behavior over horizontal, layer-by-layer tickets.

source.quote: - Prefer vertical slices that produce independently verifiable behavior.

trigger: tickets are being drafted for a body of work
outcome: each ticket is independently demonstrable rather than one layer of a larger change
rationale: A ticket-sizing/shaping principle applied via judgment throughout to-tickets (and echoed by wayfinder's own sizing rule) rather than enforced as a single deterministic step, so shared-context rather than helper.

statement: Size each ticket to fit inside one fresh agent context/session.

source.quote: - Keep each ticket small enough for one fresh agent context.

trigger: tickets are being drafted
outcome: tickets are executable by one agent session without carrying prior context
notes: Same sizing principle as wayfinder's ticket sizing (BU-P4-071); cross-reference for shared-context-map.
rationale: Judging what 'fits inside one fresh agent context' is a size/scope call made repeatedly while drafting tickets, and the same discipline recurs in wayfinder (BU-P4-080) -- shared-context, not a mechanical helper step.

statement: Assign exactly one owning repository to every implementation ticket; represent cross-repository delivery with explicit counterpart tickets and a stated merge order rather than one ambiguous shared ticket.

source.quote:
- Assign exactly one owning repository to each implementation ticket.
- Represent cross-repository delivery with counterpart tickets and explicit merge
  order, not one ambiguous shared ticket.

trigger: a ticket spans or touches more than one repository
outcome: ownership stays unambiguous even for cross-repository work
notes: Reused by the cross-repo-work skill (P5 partition candidate) as its own repository-ownership premise.
rationale: Deciding ownership and how to represent a cross-repository dependency is a judgment call applied throughout ticket drafting, reused as cross-repo-work's own premise -- shared-context rather than a deterministic helper.

statement: Never create a ticket that duplicates an existing td task or GitHub issue; update the existing one instead.

source.quote: - Never duplicate an existing td task or GitHub issue.

trigger: a candidate ticket may already exist in the tracker
outcome: the tracker has no duplicate tickets for the same outcome
rationale: Recognizing whether a candidate ticket duplicates an existing tracked item requires judgment (matching intent, not just text), applied throughout drafting -- shared-context, not a mechanical helper check.

statement: A ticket is not considered ready to publish unless its acceptance criteria are genuinely observable and its stated blockers are accurate.

source.quote:
- A ticket is not ready unless its acceptance criteria are observable and its
  blockers are accurate.

trigger: a ticket is about to be published
outcome: only tickets meeting the readiness bar are published
rationale: A readiness bar judged against each ticket's specific acceptance criteria and blockers -- discretionary, not a fixed mechanical test -- applied throughout drafting, so shared-context rather than helper.

statement: When loading project context for ticket authoring, do not automatically add td instructions to a repository's own guidance files as a side effect.

source.quote: Do not automatically add td instructions to repository guidance files.

trigger: project context is being loaded, and the repo lacks td instructions
outcome: the repository's own guidance files are left untouched unless explicitly requested
notes: A restraint rule limiting incidental side effects of the workflow.
rationale: A restraint specific to the load-project-context stage's own side effects (don't touch repo guidance files while loading context) -- stage-scoped guidance, not a general reusable helper action.

statement: Create a short investigation ticket only when a genuinely blocking unknown cannot be answered from existing evidence, and that ticket must name the exact decision or artifact it is meant to produce.

source.quote:
Create a short investigation ticket only when an unknown cannot be answered from
existing evidence. Investigation tickets must name the decision or artifact they
produce.

trigger: an unknown is identified while drafting a ticket breakdown
outcome: investigation tickets are created sparingly and each has a named deliverable
rationale: Deciding whether an unknown is 'genuinely blocking' and naming its exact deliverable is a judgment call made specifically while extracting decisions and unknowns in this stage, not a deterministic helper step.

statement: Do not split one behavior into separate horizontal tickets such as 'write backend', 'write frontend', and 'add tests'; keep it as one vertical-slice ticket.

source.quote:
- Do not create separate "write backend", "write frontend", and "add tests"
  horizontal tickets for one behavior.

trigger: tickets are being drafted for one behavior
outcome: the behavior stays represented by one demoable ticket instead of fragmented layer tickets
rationale: The vertical-slice discipline (no horizontal layer tickets) is a judgment applied while drafting tickets in this stage, but the same rule underlies the whole to-tickets discipline (BU-P4-059), so shared-context rather than a mechanical, stage-local helper.

statement: For a mechanical change too wide to land as one vertical slice, use expand-migrate-contract: add the new form beside the old, migrate callers in bounded green batches, then remove the old form; migrate tickets are blocked by expand, and the contract ticket is blocked by every migration ticket.

source.quote:
1. **Expand**: add the new form beside the old.
2. **Migrate**: move callers in bounded, green batches.
3. **Contract**: remove the old form after every migration ticket completes.

Declare all migrate tickets blocked by expand, and contract blocked by every
migration ticket.

trigger: one mechanical change would break too many callers to land as a single vertical slice
outcome: the refactor lands as a dependency-ordered expand/migrate/contract sequence instead of one unsafe wide change
notes: A named, portable technique -- likely reusable outside to-tickets for any wide mechanical refactor.
rationale: Names a fixed, portable technique (expand-migrate-contract) with a deterministic dependency-wiring rule once chosen -- mechanical once invoked, and reusable by any wide mechanical refactor beyond to-tickets (per its own note), so shared-helper rather than a workflow-local helper or a judgment-bearing stage-context.

statement: Unless the user explicitly asked to publish immediately, present the proposed ticket breakdown first and ask only whether granularity, ownership, and blocking edges are correct -- do not re-ask about decisions already made.

source.quote:
Unless the user explicitly said to create or publish tickets immediately, present
the proposed breakdown first. For every ticket show:

1. Title and owning repo.
2. Epic.
3. Blocked by.
4. What it delivers.
5. Acceptance criteria summary.

Ask only whether granularity, ownership, and blocking edges are correct. Do not ask
the user to reconfirm decisions already made.

trigger: a candidate ticket breakdown has been drafted
outcome: the user confirms structural correctness before tickets are published
notes: A needs_input-style checkpoint, structurally similar to to-spec's seam confirmation (BU-P4-053).
rationale: A user-confirmation checkpoint specific to the confirm-breakdown stage's own flow (ask only about structure, not settled decisions) -- requires judging what is already decided versus what is still open, not a mechanical helper step.

statement: When a matching task already exists, update it (parent, log entry) rather than creating a duplicate.

source.quote:
For an existing task, update rather than duplicate it:

```bash
td update <id> --parent <epic-id>
td log <id> "Preserved branch/PR/worktree and cross-repo counterpart details"
```

trigger: a ticket to publish matches an existing tracked task
outcome: the existing task is updated in place instead of a duplicate being created
rationale: Recognizing a 'matching' existing task requires judgment (not exact-match lookup), applied while publishing -- and the same anti-duplication discipline is stated as a to-tickets Principle (BU-P4-062), so shared-context rather than a mechanical helper.

statement: Do not mark newly published tasks in_progress; that transition belongs to dispatch or the worker that later starts the work. New tickets remain open until execution actually begins.

source.quote:
Do not mark tasks `in_progress`; dispatch or a worker does that. New published tasks
remain `open` until work begins.

trigger: tickets/epics are being published to td
outcome: ticket status accurately reflects that planning, not execution, has occurred
notes: Parallels sergeant-rs's own 'Work state is not process state' invariant: planning authority and execution authority stay separate, enforced here by the actor's own convention rather than by any runtime.
rationale: A policy convention enforced by the actor, not a claim that the runtime must own this ordering -- no engine dependency implied.

statement: td dependencies are repository-local; for cross-repository blockers, record the counterpart repo/ticket id and exact merge order in both descriptions/logs rather than inventing a native dependency edge td cannot enforce across separate databases.

source.quote:
td dependencies are repository-local. For cross-repository blockers:

- Record the counterpart repo and td ID in both descriptions or logs.
- State the exact merge order.
- Do not invent a native dependency edge that td cannot enforce across databases.

trigger: a ticket is blocked by a ticket in a different repository's td database
outcome: cross-repo blocking is tracked honestly as a documented convention, not a fabricated native edge
notes: An honest acknowledgment of a limitation in the external tool (td), not a claim that Sergeant's own engine must fix cross-database dependency edges.
rationale: A publish-to-td-specific convention for working around td's per-repository limitation -- stage-scoped guidance for how this one stage records cross-repo blockers, not a reusable mechanical action outside that stage.

statement: When reporting the dispatch frontier, recommend one worker per owning repository as the default concurrency, unless the project explicitly supports more.

source.quote:
- Recommended concurrency: one worker per owning repository unless the project
  explicitly supports more.

trigger: the dispatch frontier is being reported after publication
outcome: a sensible default concurrency is recommended alongside the frontier
rationale: A default-with-override recommendation made specifically while reporting the frontier in this stage -- requires judging whether the project 'explicitly supports more' concurrency, not a fixed mechanical output.

statement: Do not actually dispatch any ticket unless the user asked to begin implementation; reporting the frontier is not itself authorization to start work.

source.quote: Do not dispatch unless the user asked to begin implementation.

trigger: the dispatch frontier and next commands have been reported
outcome: publication and reporting never silently trigger execution
notes: A restraint rule separating planning output from execution authorization.
rationale: A restraint rule scoped to the report-frontier stage's own output (reporting is not authorization) -- governs what this stage must not do, not a reusable mechanical helper step.

statement: Close stale duplicate tickets only alongside an explicit note naming the canonical superseding task.

source.quote:
7. Close stale duplicates only with an explicit superseding task:

```bash
td close <duplicate-id> --admin "Superseded by <canonical-id>"
```

trigger: a stale duplicate ticket is found during graph validation
outcome: closures are traceable to the canonical ticket rather than leaving an unexplained closure
rationale: Judging that a ticket is truly a 'stale duplicate' and naming its canonical replacement is discretionary, and the same anti-duplication discipline recurs elsewhere in to-tickets (BU-P4-062, BU-P4-069) -- shared-context rather than a mechanical helper.

statement: Wayfinder plans a body of work too large for one agent session as a shared map of decision tickets on the issue tracker, resolving them one at a time until the way to a named destination is clear.

source.quote: description: Plan a huge chunk of work — more than one agent session can hold — as a shared map of decision tickets on your issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear.

trigger: an idea is too large and unclear for one agent session to plan directly
outcome: a durable, incrementally-resolved decision map exists on the issue tracker
rationale: Clear trigger, bounded outcome (destination reached, no tickets remain), and a completion condition -- the §6.2 test -- even though its two modes (chart/resolve) recur across many independent sessions.
alternatives_considered: stage (rejected: wayfinder has its own independent trigger — an idea too large for one session — and its own durable completion condition, not a step entered from inside another workflow)

engine-gap (rejected: the top-level trigger/outcome pair itself needs no new runtime capability to represent; the actual engine gap is the dynamically-discovered ticket graph resolving a ticket produces, captured separately at BU-P4-090)

statement: Wayfinder defaults to planning only: each ticket resolves a decision and the map is done once nothing is left to decide, not once the underlying work is executed; an effort may explicitly override this default in its own Notes to carry execution into the map.

source.quote: Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

trigger: a wayfinder map is being charted or worked
outcome: the map stays scoped to decisions unless the effort explicitly opts into carrying execution
rationale: A scope-default governing how the whole map behaves (plan vs. execute), decided once during chartering and then applied throughout -- it is guidance the chart-map stage's actor follows, not itself a separate durable checkpoint with its own pass/fail outcome, so stage-context rather than promoting it to its own stage.

statement: In narration and on the map, refer to every map and ticket by its name (title), never by a bare id or number, because a wall of bare ids is illegible while names read at a glance; the id/URL still rides inside the name as a link.

source.quote: Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride *inside* the name, never stand in for it.

trigger: a map or ticket is referenced in narration or on the map
outcome: humans read a legible name rather than an opaque id
rationale: A narration/legibility convention judged in the moment (choose the readable name, not the bare id) whenever anything is referenced, not a deterministic lookup -- and it is a general authoring habit rather than one wayfinder-specific mechanical step, so shared-context over helper.

statement: A wayfinder map is exactly one issue on the tracker, labeled wayfinder:map, and is the canonical artifact; its decision tickets are child issues of that map.

source.quote: The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

trigger: a wayfinder effort is chartered
outcome: there is exactly one canonical, discoverable map artifact per effort
rationale: A fixed structural fact about the map artifact (one issue, one label, children are child issues) -- deterministic and specific to wayfinder's own map convention, not a rule other workflows reuse, so helper rather than shared-helper.

statement: The map is an index, not a store: it gists and links to each closed ticket's answer but never restates the decision itself, so each decision lives in exactly one place.

source.quote: The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

trigger: a decision has been resolved and needs to be reflected on the map
outcome: the map stays a lightweight index rather than duplicating ticket content
notes: Parallels sergeant-rs's own 'journal is truth, projections are disposable' shape: one authoritative record per fact, everything else is a pointer.
rationale: A fixed content-boundary rule for the map artifact (index, not store) -- deterministic and wayfinder-specific, not shared by other workflows' artifacts, so helper rather than shared-helper.

statement: Each wayfinder ticket's body is sized to fit one 100K-token agent session.

source.quote: Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

trigger: a decision ticket is being created
outcome: any single ticket is resolvable within one bounded agent session
notes: Same sizing discipline as to-tickets' 'small enough for one fresh agent context' (BU-P4-060).
rationale: A sizing judgment ('fits one 100K-token session') applied whenever a ticket is drafted, and the identical sizing discipline recurs in to-tickets (BU-P4-060) -- shared-context, not a mechanical per-ticket helper check.

statement: Every wayfinder ticket carries one of four type labels (research, prototype, grilling, task), which determines how it gets resolved.

source.quote: Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

trigger: a decision ticket is created
outcome: the ticket's resolution path is determined by an explicit, machine-readable type label
rationale: A fixed, deterministic classification fact (every ticket carries exactly one of four labels) specific to wayfinder's own ticket format, not a convention reused by other workflows' tickets, so helper rather than shared-helper.

statement: A session claims a wayfinder ticket by assigning it to the driving developer before doing any work; assignment is the sole claim signal, so an open unassigned ticket is unclaimed and a claimed one is skipped by other concurrent sessions.

source.quote: A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

trigger: multiple sessions may work the same map concurrently
outcome: concurrent sessions do not duplicate work on the same ticket
notes: Primary supporting evidence for BU-P4-090's engine-gap finding: the concurrency-admission primitive ('claim') lives entirely on the external tracker's assignment field, outside any Sergeant-owned durable state.
rationale: The claim mechanism itself (assignment on the external tracker) is a deterministic, mechanical action taken at the start of resolve-ticket -- representable today as an ordinary helper invocation against the tracker's own field, not evidence on its own that the engine needs a new capability; it becomes supporting evidence for BU-P4-090's consolidated engine-gap only in combination with the other wayfinder concurrency facts, not individually.

statement: Ticket blocking uses the tracker's own native dependency relationship (so the frontier is visible in the tracker's UI without opening the map); a ticket is unblocked once every ticket blocking it is closed, and the frontier is the set of open, unblocked, unclaimed tickets.

source.quote: Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship — essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children — the edge of the known.

trigger: the map's current workable tickets need to be identified
outcome: the frontier is computed from native blocking state, not from an internal Sergeant record
notes: Second piece of supporting evidence for BU-P4-090's engine-gap finding.
rationale: Computing the frontier from the tracker's native blocking relationship is today a deterministic query against an external system, not something Sergeant's own engine must compute -- a helper action, and (like BU-P4-082) supporting evidence for the consolidated engine-gap (BU-P4-090) only in combination with the other facts, not an independent gap by itself.

statement: A resolved ticket's answer is not part of its body; it is recorded on resolution, and any assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue rather than pasted into it.

source.quote: The answer isn't part of the body — it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

trigger: a ticket is being resolved
outcome: the ticket's question and its answer/assets stay in separate, clearly-timed places
notes: Parallels sergeant-rs's own blob-store convention (large payloads referenced by content address, not inlined into the journal).
rationale: A fixed, deterministic sequencing rule for where a ticket's answer and assets live -- specific to wayfinder's own resolve-ticket convention, not a rule other workflows' helpers reuse, so helper rather than shared-helper.

statement: Every wayfinder ticket is either HITL (resolved through a live exchange with a human who speaks for themselves) or AFK (resolved by the agent alone); on a HITL ticket the agent must never answer on the human's behalf.

source.quote: Every ticket is either **HITL** — human in the loop, worked *with* a human who speaks for themselves — or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

trigger: a ticket is about to be resolved
outcome: human-authority decisions are never silently answered by the agent
notes: A hard authority-boundary rule, echoing sergeant-setup's consent-gating concerns (P5 partition) and needs_input semantics generally.
rationale: A hard authority boundary (HITL vs AFK, never answer for the human) that the resolve-ticket stage's actor must judge and respect for every ticket -- specific to how wayfinder classifies and resolves its own tickets, not a general-purpose rule reused outside wayfinder, so stage-context rather than shared-context.

statement: A research-type wayfinder ticket surfaces a fact a decision is waiting on by reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local knowledge bases, and is resolved by delegating to a research subagent.

source.quote: - **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a `/research` **subagent**. Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.

trigger: a research-type ticket is chosen for resolution
outcome: the fact-finding work is delegated to a dedicated research procedure rather than performed ad hoc
notes: Cross-references the research skill (P3 partition) -- reuse via ordinary actor-stage delegation, fully expressible today without any engine change (proposal §7.5-7.6).
rationale: Describes how the resolve-ticket stage handles one specific ticket type (research) by delegating to another skill -- stage-scoped routing guidance rather than a rule reused independently of wayfinder's own ticket-type dispatch, so stage-context rather than shared-context.

statement: A task-type wayfinder ticket is manual work that must happen before a decision can be made (e.g. provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen); it is the one ticket type that does rather than decides, and it earns its place only by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination itself.

source.quote: - **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a *decision* can be made — nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that *does* rather than decides — and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the hum

trigger: an unblocking prerequisite exists that is not itself a decision
outcome: the prerequisite is tracked and resolved as a task, without expanding the map's scope to include delivery work
rationale: Describes how the resolve-ticket stage handles the task ticket type (do, don't decide) -- part of wayfinder's own ticket-type dispatch logic for that stage, not a generic rule reused elsewhere, so stage-context rather than shared-context.

statement: The map is deliberately incomplete: only decisions sharp enough to phrase precisely become tickets now, and everything else that's foreseeable but not yet phraseable stays recorded loosely as fog rather than being pre-sliced into ticket-sized pieces.

source.quote: The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

trigger: charting or updating a map
outcome: the map never overcommits to decisions that aren't yet specifiable
rationale: Describes the standing discipline that governs the whole chart-map stage's behavior (ticket now vs. fog later) rather than being itself a separate checkpoint with its own pass/fail outcome -- it is guidance the chart-map stage follows throughout, so stage-context rather than a second stage.

statement: Whether something belongs in a ticket or in the fog is decided by whether the question can already be stated precisely, not by whether it can already be answered.

source.quote: **Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now — _not_ whether you can answer it now.

trigger: deciding whether a foreseen decision should become a ticket now or stay in the fog
outcome: ticket-vs-fog placement is decided by a consistent, explicit test
rationale: The fog-vs-ticket test is a judgment call the actor applies whenever the question arises during charting, not a deterministic check with one mechanical answer, so stage-context rather than helper.

statement: Resolving a wayfinder ticket clears the fog immediately ahead of it, graduating whatever is now specifiable into fresh child tickets one at a time, until no tickets remain and the way to the destination is clear.

source.quote: The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

trigger: a decision ticket has just been resolved
outcome: the map's ticket set grows dynamically as the effort proceeds, rather than being fixed at chartering time
notes: Consolidated engine-gap finding for the wayfinder workflow's dynamically-discovered decision graph; see engine_gap for the full template. Supporting evidence: BU-P4-082 (cooperative claim-by-assignment), BU-P4-083 (native-tracker blocking/frontier), BU-P4-084 (answer recorded on resolution, not in body), BU-P4-098 (concurrent sessions expected).
rationale: The ordered-stage-list workflow model (§13.1: a resolved WorkflowDefinition with a fixed stage list journaled in workflow.bound before execution, per proposal §3.3/§13.1) requires the full stage sequence to be pinned before Work starts. Wayfinder's ticket graph is discovered incrementally: resolving one ticket can graduate zero, one, or several new child tickets whose existence was not knowable when the map was chartered. No lower rung represents this faithfully.
alternatives_considered: stage (rejected: a stage's execution is one bounded turn/session and the parent's stage list is pinned before the Work starts, per proposal §3.3/§13.1; wayfinder's ticket graph is discovered incrementally across many independently-chosen sessions, so there is no fixed stage list to pin)

shared-context (rejected: this is what wayfinder does today — claim state, blocking graph, and resolution history all live on the external tracker, outside Sergeant's journal, so the runtime has no evidence of them and cannot recover, resume, or report on them)

helper (rejected: a helper is a deterministic invocation; graduating fresh child tickets and refusing a second concurrent claim on the same ticket both need a live, journaled claim/admission primitive the runtime doesn't have, not a fixed script)

engine_gap.behavior: A durable procedure whose full set of sub-checkpoints (decision tickets) is not known in advance: it is discovered incrementally as prior checkpoints resolve, each checkpoint may be claimed and worked by an independently-chosen session (fresh agent context), concurrent sessions must not duplicate work on the same checkpoint, and checkpoints form a dependency graph (blocking edges) computed live rather than declared as one fixed order.
